stats.starsTooltip: Total number of stars (favorites) the repository received on GitHub.
stats.forksTooltip: Number of repository copies (forks) created by other users.
stats.openIssuesTooltip: Number of issues (problems or requests) that are still open in the repository.
stats.closedIssuesTooltip: Total closed issues. The percentage is the closed share of all issues (open + closed) and includes issues closed as "not planned" or duplicates.
stats.codeChurnTooltip: Lines added divided by lines removed over the last {{weeks}} weeks. It describes the kind of change (more new code or more cleanup); it doesn't measure quality. Requires at least {{min}} weeks with activity.
stats.leadTimeTooltip: Median time between a Pull Request's creation and its merge, over up to {{n}} most recent merged PRs (bots excluded). The median isn't skewed by a few very slow PRs; p90 shows the tail (90% were merged within that time).
stats.divergenceTooltip: Average comments by people (general and code review) per PR, over up to {{n}} most recent merged PRs. Bot comments and bot PRs don't count. Requires a GitHub token.

stats.reviewCoverageSample: approved by someone else · {{reviewed}}% with any review · {{n}} PRs
stats.reviewCoverageTooltip: Share of the up to {{n}} most recent merged PRs (bots excluded) approved (Approve) by someone else before merging. The second number counts any review by someone else (approval, change request or review comment). Projects that approve by command or bot (e.g. /lgtm) show low coverage.
stats.firstReviewNone: No PR reviewed by someone else
stats.firstReviewTooltip: Median (and p90) time from the PR being ready for review (or created, if it was never a draft; the first "ready" counts) to the first review by someone else before the merge, over recent merged PRs that got a review. A review made while still a draft counts as zero wait. Plain comments, which aren't reviews, don't count.
stats.prSizeTooltip: Changed lines (added + removed) per PR, over recent merged PRs. Small PRs (under {{max}} lines) are easier to review well. Generated files (e.g. lockfiles) are counted.
stats.ciHealthTooltip: Success rate of the latest GitHub Actions runs triggered by pushes to the default branch (up to 50). Success counts against failure, timeout and startup failure; cancelled and skipped runs are left out. Scheduled, Dependabot and pull request runs aren't counted; pushes made by bots are. CI outside GitHub Actions (Travis, CircleCI…) isn't shown here.
stats.conventionalCommitsTooltip: Share of recent default-branch commits (up to 100, no merges, no bots) whose first line follows Conventional Commits: type(scope)!: description, with the types feat, fix, docs, style, refactor, perf, test, build, ci, chore and revert.
stats.releaseCadenceTooltip: Releases published on GitHub in the last 12 months (dated by the tag, or by publication if the tag is later), median interval between days with a release in that period (two lines released the same day count as one day), days since the latest, and share of SemVer tags (e.g. v1.2.3, package@1.2.3) among the latest 100. Projects that only push tags, without releases, aren't shown here.

detectors.tests: Looks for test/, tests/, __tests__/ folders and *.test.js/ts(x), *.spec.*, test_*.py, *_test.go, *_spec.rb, src/test/ files.
detectors.ciCd: Looks for CI configuration: GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, CircleCI, Jenkinsfile, Azure Pipelines, Travis, Buildkite, Bitbucket, Drone, AppVeyor.
detectors.docker: Looks for a Dockerfile (including Dockerfile.* and in subfolders), Containerfile and docker-compose/compose.yml.
detectors.linter: Looks for linter configuration at the root, one level down or in packages/, apps/, crates/…: ESLint (incl. eslint.config.js), Biome, golangci-lint, Ruff, Flake8, Pylint, RuboCop, Clippy, Stylelint, SwiftLint, Checkstyle, Sonar. Configuration inside pyproject.toml (Ruff) or package.json (eslintConfig) isn't detected.

about.title: About Bisolhador
about.description: Bisolhador is an analytical tool for evaluating GitHub repositories like a Tech Lead. It analyzes volume, governance, maturity, and activity metrics to provide insights about project health and efficiency.

token.title: Why configure a Token?
token.description: Without a token, GitHub limits to 60 requests per hour. With a Personal Access Token, you can make up to 5,000 requests per hour, allowing more complete analyses.

warning.message: The token is saved only in your browser and is never sent to our servers. Your privacy is protected.

busFactor.title: Bus Factor
busFactor.tooltip: Minimum number of people who together make 70% of the commits (no bots, same window as the table below). The lower, the more the project depends on few people. A simple heuristic, not the academic "truck factor" (which uses file authorship).

guide.title: How to read the indicators
guide.intro: For each indicator: what it measures, how to read it, what it doesn't say, and the matching metric from CHAOSS, the Linux Foundation project that defines open source community health metrics. When Bisolhador measures differently from CHAOSS, the difference is written down. No single indicator measures quality: use them to ask questions about a project, not to grade it.
guide.ethics: CHAOSS warns that health metrics can expose people. When using per-person or per-team indicators (for example, in a classroom), read the CHAOSS data ethics guidance.
guide.ethicsLink: CHAOSS privacy and data ethics recommendations

stars-forks.name: Stars and forks
stars-forks.what: How many people starred the repository and how many copies (forks) exist.
stars-forks.read: A sign of visibility and interest, not of use or quality. Course and tutorial repositories often have many stars.
stars-forks.limits: Stars don't expire: an abandoned project keeps the ones it had.
stars-forks.chaossNote: CHAOSS suggests combining several signals (stars, forks, new contributors, clones, dependents); only stars and forks are shown here.

languages.name: Languages
languages.what: Each language's share of the repository's code, according to GitHub.
languages.read: Shows the tech stack and who could contribute.
languages.limits: Detected by GitHub's Linguist, which already ignores generated, vendored and documentation files; files it doesn't recognise as such can still inflate a language. Languages under 1% are grouped as "Others".
languages.chaossNote: CHAOSS measures by number of files or lines per language; GitHub reports bytes.

issues.name: Open, closed and % closed issues
issues.what: Total open and closed issues (GitHub search) and the closed share of all issues.
issues.read: A high closed share suggests a cared-for backlog; many open issues may just mean a popular project.
issues.limits: Whole history, including issues closed as "not planned" or duplicates: it's a closing rate, not a resolution rate.
issues.chaossNote: CHAOSS (Issues Closed) also proposes the closed/total ratio, but per period; here it covers the whole history.

prs-merges.name: PRs and merges
prs-merges.what: Total pull requests and accepted (merged) PRs.
prs-merges.read: Shows the volume of proposed and accepted contributions.
prs-merges.limits: Volume says nothing about contribution quality.
prs-merges.chaossNote: Whole-history totals; CHAOSS (Change Requests, Change Requests Accepted) counts per period.

lead-time.name: Lead time
lead-time.what: Median time from opening a PR to merging it, over the up to 50 most recent merged PRs, bots excluded. p90 shows the tail: 90% were merged within that time.
lead-time.read: A low lead time means a fast integration cycle. Compare with p90: a big gap means some PRs get forgotten.
lead-time.limits: Merged PRs only (closed without merge aren't counted). Small maintenance PRs pull the median down. PRs opened by AI agents are left out and show up in "AI in the Process".
lead-time.chaossNote: Same question and aggregation (median, accepted PRs only). The sample differs: CHAOSS selects PRs created in a period; here it is the up to 50 most recently merged, bots excluded.

review-coverage.name: Review coverage
review-coverage.what: Share of recent merged PRs approved by someone else before merging, and share with any review by someone else.
review-coverage.read: Shows whether the project practices formal review. The "Unapproved" badge is the complement.
review-coverage.limits: Only GitHub's formal review counts: projects that approve by command or bot (/lgtm) show low coverage. Requires a token. PRs opened by AI agents are left out and show up in "AI in the Process".
review-coverage.chaossNote: CHAOSS (Change Request Reviews) doesn't define a single formula; Self-Merge Rates counts PRs merged by their author without review. Here it counts the lack of approval by someone else, whoever merged (self-merge is in the badge tooltip).

first-review.name: Time to first review
first-review.what: Median (and p90) time from the PR being ready for review to the first review by someone else before merging.
first-review.read: How long contributors wait for feedback. Long waits discourage contributions.
first-review.limits: Merged PRs that got a review only. A review made while still a draft counts as zero wait. Plain comments don't count. Requires a token. PRs opened by AI agents are left out and show up in "AI in the Process".
first-review.chaossNote: CHAOSS (Change Request Review Duration) starts at submission and suggests the mean; here the clock starts when the PR is ready for review (a draft isn't waiting) and the median is used, less sensitive to a few forgotten PRs. Time to First Response counts any response, comments included; here only formal reviews count.

pr-size.name: PR size
pr-size.what: Median changed lines (added + removed) per recent merged PR, and share of PRs under 400 lines.
pr-size.read: Small PRs get reviewed more carefully and merged faster. It's one of the easiest practices to teach.
pr-size.limits: Generated files (lockfiles, snapshots) count as lines. Requires a token. PRs opened by AI agents are left out and show up in "AI in the Process".
pr-size.chaossNote: CHAOSS (Code Changes Lines) sums the lines touched per period, from commits; here it is per PR.

divergence.name: Divergence
divergence.what: Average comments by people (general and review) per recent merged PR.
divergence.read: Little discussion may mean simple PRs or shallow review; a lot may mean large or unclear PRs.
divergence.limits: Doesn't tell productive discussion from conflict. Bot comments don't count. Requires a token. PRs opened by AI agents are left out and show up in "AI in the Process".
divergence.chaossNote: There's no equivalent CHAOSS metric; the closest is Change Request Reviews, which includes comments as part of review.

ci-health.name: CI health
ci-health.what: Success rate and median duration of the latest 50 GitHub Actions runs triggered by pushes to the default branch.
ci-health.read: High success and short duration mean CI is taken seriously. Frequent failures on the default branch mean broken code is being merged.
ci-health.limits: GitHub Actions only (Travis, CircleCI etc. aren't shown). The latest 50 completed runs triggered by pushes; cancelled and skipped ones are left out, so n can be under 50. Scheduled, Dependabot and pull request runs aren't counted; pushes made by bots to the default branch are.
ci-health.chaossNote: There's no CHAOSS metric for CI health.

conventional-commits.name: Conventional Commits
conventional-commits.what: Share of recent default-branch commits (no merges, no bots) whose first line follows type(scope)!: description.
conventional-commits.read: Shows commit message discipline, which enables a readable history, automatic changelogs and versioning.
conventional-commits.limits: Only the common types (feat, fix, docs…) count. Projects with their own convention (e.g. "subsystem: message", like the Linux kernel) show a low share, close to 0%.
conventional-commits.chaossNote: There's no CHAOSS metric for message conventions; Code Changes Commits mentions consistently structured messages as a prerequisite for filtering commits by type.

release-cadence.name: Release cadence
release-cadence.what: Releases published on GitHub in the last 12 months (dated by the tag, or by publication if the tag is later), median interval between release days, days since the latest and share of SemVer tags among the latest 100.
release-cadence.read: Regular releases suggest a live, predictable project; SemVer tells users the impact of each version.
release-cadence.limits: Projects that only push tags, without GitHub releases, aren't shown. The right frequency depends on the kind of project.
release-cadence.chaossNote: CHAOSS (Release Frequency) counts releases per period (week, month, year); here it is 12 months, with the median interval between release days.

health-score.name: Health Score
health-score.what: Share of 7 items present: README, license, CONTRIBUTING, description, code of conduct, issue template and PR template.
health-score.read: Shows whether the project is ready to welcome newcomers.
health-score.limits: Only checks that the files exist, not that they're good or up to date.
health-score.chaossNote: CHAOSS covers these aspects in separate, deeper metrics: Licenses Declared (licenses declared in the files), Code of Conduct for a Project (quality and enforcement of the code of conduct) and Documentation Discoverability (a member survey on how easy the documentation is to find).

maturity.name: Engineering maturity
maturity.what: Whether the repository has tests, CI, Docker and a linter configured (from its file list), and whether PRs are merged without approval.
maturity.read: Shows engineering practices in place. "?" means it couldn't be checked, not that it doesn't exist.
maturity.limits: Detects presence, not quality: a single placeholder test file is enough to show "tests".
maturity.chaossNote: CHAOSS (Test Coverage) measures the share of code exercised by tests; here it only detects whether tests exist.

zombie-branches.name: Zombie branches
zombie-branches.what: Branches with no commits for more than 90 days, excluding the default, protected and long-lived branches (release, maintenance, develop, stable, gh-pages, lines like 5.x or v4).
zombie-branches.read: Many zombie branches suggest abandoned work or no repository cleanup.
zombie-branches.limits: Requires a token to check each branch's last commit date. The scan stops at 1,000 branches, and then the number is a minimum.
zombie-branches.chaossNote: CHAOSS (Branch Lifecycle) looks at how branches are created, merged, kept and deleted; here only stale ones are counted.

ai-tools.name: Detected AI tools
ai-tools.what: AI tools with some trace in the repository, each with where the evidence comes from: config (a versioned configuration file, such as CLAUDE.md, .github/copilot-instructions.md or .cursorrules), commit (co-authorship declared in a Co-authored-by trailer, or a commit authored by an agent), PR (a merged PR opened by an agent) and review (a review or comment by an AI review bot). AGENTS.md and .mcp.json show up as "Agents (generic)", since they serve several tools.
ai-tools.read: Answers whether the project guides AI agents, and with which tools. The same tool from several sources suggests consistent use; config alone may be an unused setup or one person's. Configuration marked "from template" came from the template repository: it is listed, but doesn't count as the repository's own use.
ai-tools.limits: It's a lower bound: "No AI traces found" doesn't mean no AI was used. Autocomplete leaves no mark, not every tool writes a co-author trailer, and personal agent bots (custom GitHub Apps) can't be classified: they count as maintenance bots. Co-authorship is recognized by the trailer's e-mail, not by the name, which anyone can type; a git name only identifies an agent when it ends in [bot]. Tools come from a fixed registry (version 2026-10-25): tools outside it don't show up. On the Dashboard, configuration is searched across the whole file tree (left unverified when the tree comes back truncated); in Classroom mode, only at the root and in known directories (.github, .claude, .cursor, .gemini, .junie…), so a CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md in a subfolder doesn't show up. Template origin is only checked with a token. On the Dashboard, a private template isn't read: the origin stays unverified. Repositories created by GitHub Classroom: GitHub doesn't report their template; on the Dashboard, the origin of configuration files stays "unverified" when Classroom's initial commit is in the 100-commit sample (outside it, they count as the repository's own); in Classroom mode, it is checked through each file's history. In Classroom mode, a file counts as the team's own configuration only when its whole history was read (up to 10 files per repository, top-level ones first); the others keep an unverified origin.
ai-tools.chaossNote: There's no equivalent CHAOSS metric for AI traces.

ai-config-depth.name: Configuration depth
ai-config-depth.what: For each configured tool: instructions only (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, .github/copilot-instructions.md, .cursor/rules/…) or instructions + extensions (skills, commands and subagents in .claude/, prompts in .github/prompts/, MCP servers in .mcp.json). A tool with any extension path shows as instructions + extensions even without an instructions file (for example, only .mcp.json or only .github/prompts/). With a token, it also shows ignored local use: .gitignore lines that hide AI artifacts (.claude/, CLAUDE.local.md, .cursor/, .cursorrules, .aider*).
ai-config-depth.read: Instructions guide the agent; extensions point to a more elaborate workflow around it. Ignored local use is a trace of AI used on someone's machine without versioning the configuration.
ai-config-depth.limits: Detects that the files exist, not what they say or whether they are followed. A line such as .claude/ in .gitignore may come from a copied .gitignore template. .gitignore is only read with a token (without one, it stays unverified), and negation lines (!) don't count. In Classroom mode, only the root and known directories are checked.
ai-config-depth.chaossNote: There's no equivalent CHAOSS metric for AI tool configuration.

ai-commits.name: Commits with AI traces
ai-commits.what: Share of the analyzed commits with declared AI co-authorship (a Co-authored-by trailer with the e-mail of a tool in the registry) or authored by an agent (Copilot, claude[bot], Devin…), always with n ("12 of 100 commits"). Merges and maintenance bots (Dependabot, Renovate, github-actions) are left out; agent commits are included. It also shows the date of the first trace in the sample.
ai-commits.read: Shows how much recent work was declared as done with AI. The first trace is the oldest in the sample, not in the repository: adoption may be earlier.
ai-commits.limits: Lower bound: only what was declared counts. Autocomplete leaves no mark, not every tool writes the trailer, whoever commits can turn it off, and a squash merge can rewrite the messages. Co-authorship is matched by e-mail, case-insensitively, never by name alone; for generic e-mails (Gemini's noreply@google.com, opencode's ai@local), the name is required too. An agent-authored commit is also recognized by the agent's e-mail in the registry (such as Copilot's or Devin's noreply); a git name only counts as an agent when it ends in [bot], and a login only on a bot account (a person whose account is called claude or copilot counts as a person); personal agent bots (custom GitHub Apps) count as maintenance and are left out. Dashboard: the latest 100 commits on the default branch. Classroom mode: default-branch commits in the period, up to the 300 most recent.
ai-commits.chaossNote: There's no equivalent CHAOSS metric. Code Changes Commits counts commits, but not AI participation.

ai-prs.name: PRs opened by agents
ai-prs.what: Share of the sampled merged PRs whose author is a coding agent in the registry (Copilot, Claude, Devin, Jules, Codex), always with n. On the Dashboard, the sample is up to the latest 50 merged PRs, people and agents together, without maintenance bots: with a token, among the 100 most recently updated merged PRs; without one, among the 100 most recently updated closed PRs. In Classroom mode, every PR merged in the period (examined up to a limit).
ai-prs.read: Shows how much of the merged work was proposed directly by an agent. Read it together with Safeguards: what matters most is whether those PRs went through human review.
ai-prs.limits: Lower bound: an agent running on someone's machine opens the PR with that person's account, and the PR counts as human. Only a bot account counts as an agent: a person whose account is called copilot or claude counts as a person. Personal agent bots (custom GitHub Apps) can't be classified and are left out, like maintenance bots. The Review dynamics indicators still measure only PRs by people; agent PRs show up only here.
ai-prs.chaossNote: There's no equivalent CHAOSS metric. Change Requests counts PRs, but doesn't tell who opened them.

ai-review.name: PRs with AI review
ai-review.what: Share of the sampled merged PRs (the same sample as PRs opened by agents) with at least one review or comment by an AI review bot in the registry (CodeRabbit, Copilot, Gemini Code Assist, Cursor, Sourcery, Greptile, Codex, Claude), always with n.
ai-review.read: Shows whether the project uses AI as a reviewer. AI review complements human approval (Safeguards and Review coverage); it doesn't replace it.
ai-review.limits: Requires a token. Only reviewers that are bots count: an AI used through a person's account shows up as a human review. On the Dashboard, each PR's reviews and comments count; in Classroom mode, only reviews (comments aren't fetched).
ai-review.chaossNote: There's no equivalent CHAOSS metric. Change Request Reviews covers reviews in general, without separating those done by AI.

ai-safeguards.name: Safeguards
ai-safeguards.what: How many merged agent PRs in the sample had no human approval (an APPROVED review before the merge, by someone who is neither the author nor a bot; the same rule as Review coverage), always with n. And the median size (changed lines) of agent PRs compared with PRs by people, in the same sample.
ai-safeguards.read: It's the indicator that matters most for teaching: did what the AI produced go through a person before getting in? Agent PRs much larger than people's are harder to review carefully.
ai-safeguards.limits: Requires a token. The count of unapproved PRs is shown even with a small n; the size comparison only appears when both groups have at least 5 PRs of known size. Projects that approve by command or bot (/lgtm) show up as unapproved. It only sees agents that open PRs with their own account (see PRs opened by agents).
ai-safeguards.chaossNote: There's no equivalent CHAOSS metric for human review of agent work.

ai-coherence.name: Sources in disagreement
ai-coherence.what: Checks, at repository level, whether the trace sources tell the same story. The block shows up when (1) there is versioned AI configuration outside the template, but no commit in the sample declares AI co-authorship or is by an agent, and no PR is by an agent; or (2) .gitignore hides AI artifacts and nothing declares use. Configuration for one tool with declarations from another is shown only as information, not as disagreement (AGENTS.md doesn't count, being generic). If the versioned .claude/settings.json turns off the co-author trailer, that is shown as a fact.
ai-coherence.read: "The sources disagree" is a starting point for a conversation, not a conclusion. The block always lists the possible legitimate causes: a squash merge that rewrites the messages, configuration set up by another group member, a tool that doesn't write the trailer, declaration turned off in the configuration.
ai-coherence.limits: The GitHub API doesn't show whether a commit message was edited: what is detected is only the incoherence between what remains. Configuration from the template repository (the template; in Classroom mode, also GitHub Classroom's initial commit) doesn't count. Repositories created by GitHub Classroom: GitHub doesn't report their template; on the Dashboard, the origin of configuration files stays "unverified" when Classroom's initial commit is in the 100-commit sample (outside it, they count as the repository's own); in Classroom mode, it is checked through each file's history. The rules only fire when the sample has commits; with an empty sample, the cross-check stays unverified. .gitignore and template origin are only checked with a token; without one, configuration counts as the repository's own. It's always about the repository, never about a person.
ai-coherence.chaossNote: There's no equivalent CHAOSS metric for coherence between AI traces.

ai-badge.name: Responsible AI use
ai-badge.what: Repository badge with five criteria: versioned AI configuration (outside the template); commits with declared co-authorship (at least one commit in the sample with an AI trace: declared co-authorship or an agent as author); coherent sources (no disagreement); agent PRs with human approval (all of those in the sample); tests and CI detected (the same as Engineering maturity). It shows "x of y" and is complete when every verifiable criterion is met.
ai-badge.read: Measures observable practices and coherence between traces, not actual AI use or anyone's character. Versioned configuration, declared AI, agent PRs reviewed by people, and tests and CI meet everything; coherence between the sources counts too. Without any AI trace, the badge is "not applicable": not using AI is never penalized.
ai-badge.limits: Criteria that don't apply (no agent PRs) or weren't verified (no token, truncated tree, empty sample) leave the denominator, so the total varies from one repository to another: read "x of y" together with the list of criteria. In Classroom mode, tests and CI are always unverified. Configuration that came only from the template doesn't make the badge apply. When the only trace is a review by an AI bot, versioned configuration and declared co-authorship don't apply: an external reviewer needs neither. The badge isn't in the Ranking and is never computed per student.
ai-badge.chaossNote: There's no equivalent CHAOSS metric. The badge follows the Health Score style (a list of items met), with its own criteria.

bus-factor.name: Bus factor and concentration
bus-factor.what: Smallest number of people responsible for 70% of the commits of the last 12 months, or of the whole history when recent activity is low (bots excluded), and the top contributor's share.
bus-factor.read: A bus factor of 1 or 2 means the project depends on very few people. Over 60% from the top contributor is critical.
bus-factor.limits: Counts commits, not reviews, issues or other contributions. Uses the whole history when GitHub's 12-month statistic is unavailable, and considers at most the top 100 contributors.
bus-factor.chaossNote: CHAOSS calls this metric Contributor Absence Factor (formerly "Bus Factor") and uses a 50% threshold; here it is 70%, so the number tends to be higher than CHAOSS's.

contributors.name: Contributors
contributors.what: Who committed most, over the last 12 months when there is enough activity (otherwise the whole history), bots excluded.
contributors.read: Shows who is sustaining the project now.
contributors.limits: Commits only: reviews, issues, documentation outside the code and mentoring don't show.
contributors.chaossNote: CHAOSS (Contributors) counts any form of participation (code, review, documentation, translation, events); here it is commits only.

commit-activity.name: Commits per week
commit-activity.what: Commits per week over the last 52 weeks, from GitHub's statistic.
commit-activity.read: Shows pace and regularity: spikes, pauses, holidays.
commit-activity.limits: Commit volume doesn't measure effort or how significant the changes are. GitHub's statistic includes merge and bot commits.
commit-activity.chaossNote: CHAOSS (Code Changes Commits) counts commits per period, optionally excluding merge and empty commits.

weekdays.name: Commits by weekday
weekdays.what: Distribution of the history's commits (no merges, up to 20k) across weekdays, in each commit author's time zone.
weekdays.read: Shows work patterns, such as projects worked on at weekends.
weekdays.limits: Includes bots (the API can't separate them). Very large repositories are capped at 20k commits.
weekdays.chaossNote: CHAOSS (Activity Dates and Times) looks at activity times in UTC and local time; here it is only the weekday of commits, in the author's local time.

add-delete.name: Additions/Deletions
add-delete.what: Lines added divided by lines removed over the last 10 weeks (at least 4 weeks with activity).
add-delete.read: Describes the kind of change: more new code or more cleanup and refactoring.
add-delete.limits: Doesn't measure quality. GitHub doesn't compute it for repositories with 10k+ commits.
add-delete.chaossNote: CHAOSS (Code Changes Lines) sums the lines touched per period; here it is the ratio of additions to deletions.

classroom.name: Classroom mode
classroom.what: The Dashboard's process indicators computed for each repository of a class within the course period: commits, active authors, concentration on the top author, merged PRs, approval by someone else, time to first review, lead time, PR size, CI health, Conventional Commits and releases. The table also has per-repository AI columns (AI tools, commits and PRs with AI traces, sources in disagreement, badge), which go into the CSV. Each row can be expanded (+) to show the repository's AI in the Process section and the Per student view: for each commit author in the period, their commits, how many declare AI co-authorship, the declared tools and the AI configuration files that person added or changed. The Per student view doesn't go into the CSV.
classroom.read: Compare teams by process, not volume: a team with few commits and small, reviewed PRs may be working better than one with many direct commits to the default branch. High concentration means one person does almost everything; worth a conversation with the team.
classroom.limits: Private repositories are analyzed only here, with the user's own token and nothing saved; the link and the CSV contain their names and numbers. Authors, concentration and Conventional Commits use up to the 300 most recent commits of the period, and PRs are examined up to a limit (marked * and +). Teams working directly on the default branch show 0 PRs and no review data. Commits and PRs don't measure effort, learning or quality, and shouldn't become automatic grades. The Per student view shows only declared use and who configured: configuring isn't using (one person may set it up for the whole group), and undeclared use doesn't show up. It's not a grade or proof. Commits made by an agent go to the agent's row, so students using cloud agents may show less declared AI. The view uses the same up to 300 commits of the period: someone whose commits all fall outside that sample doesn't appear. Configuration authorship looks at up to 50 commits per file, in up to 10 files. Nothing in the Per student view leaves the browser: it isn't in the CSV and isn't saved.
classroom.chaossNote: Each column follows the CHAOSS reference of the matching entry in this guide, computed over the chosen period. CHAOSS advises care with privacy when using per-person or per-team metrics; that's why concentration doesn't name the top author. The AI Per student view names authors by the maintainer's decision, but stays on screen only.

classroom.title: Classroom Mode
classroom.subtitle: Compare a class's team repositories over the course period: up to {{max}} repositories, public or private ones your token can access, analyzed now, with the same process indicators as the Dashboard. Nothing is saved; the class lives in this page's link.
classroom.ethics: Use it as a starting point for conversations with teams, not as an automatic grade: commits and PRs don't measure effort or learning.
classroom.needsToken: Classroom mode needs a GitHub token: each repository makes 6 to 9 requests, and without a token the limit is 60 per hour. For private repositories (e.g. GitHub Classroom), the token must have access to them.
classroom.reposPlaceholder: owner/repository or https://github.com/owner/repository — one per line
classroom.reposTruncated: Only the first {{max}} will be analyzed.
classroom.notes: Dates in UTC. "Commits" is the default-branch total in the period; authors, concentration and Conventional Commits use up to the 300 most recent commits of the period, without merges and bots. PRs: merged in the period into any branch, bots excluded. CI: up to 100 push runs on the default branch. Releases: among the latest 100. Concentration = share of the author with most commits, without naming them.

status.notFound: Repository not found (or private without access with your token).
status.error: Couldn't analyze it (API failure or rate limit).

classroom.sampledNote: * computed over a sample (the 300 most recent commits, or PRs examined up to the limit); + means the real number is higher.
classroom.invalidUrlPeriod: The period in the link is invalid. Pick the dates and analyze again.
classroom.privateNote: This class includes private repositories. The data was read with your token and stays in this browser: nothing is saved by Bisolhador. The link and the CSV contain these repositories' names and numbers; share them only with people who already have access.

import.result: {{matched}} of the organization's {{found}} repositories (archived ones left out). The list below was filled in.
import.capped: Only the first 1,000 repositories were read.
import.orgNotFound: Organization or user not found (or no access with your token).
import.orgFailed: Couldn't list the repositories (API failure or rate limit).

ai.expand: Show AI in the Process for {{repo}}
ai.collapse: Hide AI in the Process for {{repo}}
ai.coherenceTip: The AI trace sources disagree. Expand the row to see why and the legitimate causes.
ai.note: AI columns: a lower bound, only traces that are declared (co-authorship, an agent as author) or versioned (configuration). No trace does not mean no AI. Commits with AI and Agent PRs show (with AI/total). Badge: criteria met/verifiable. Expand the row (+) for the full section and the per-student detail, which does not go into the CSV.

aiProcess.title: AI in the Process
aiProcess.tooltip: Traces GitHub keeps: versioned AI agent configuration, co-authorship declared in commits, PRs opened by agents and reviews by AI bots. It does not measure how much code AI wrote.
aiProcess.hiddenOnly: No tool identified: the only trace is local use ignored in .gitignore (see Configuration depth).
aiProcess.noTracesDetail: No trace does not mean no AI: autocomplete leaves no mark, and commit co-authorship depends on the tool and on the committer's settings.
aiProcess.lowerBoundNote: Everything here is a lower bound: only AI use that left a trace in the repository shows up. No trace does not mean no use. The review and PR indicators in the other sections still measure only PRs by people; agent PRs appear only here.

tooltip.config: The tool's configuration file is versioned in the repository.
tooltip.commit: Commit with declared co-authorship (Co-authored-by trailer) or authored by an agent.
tooltip.pr: Merged PR opened by an agent.
tooltip.review: PR reviewed or commented on by an AI review bot.
tooltip.template: This tool's configuration came from the template repository: it is listed, but does not count as the repository's own use.
tooltip.templateUnknown: Could not confirm whether the configuration came from a template repository.

depth.title: Configuration depth
depth.nonePartial: No AI configuration in the checked locations.
depth.treeTruncated: ? Configuration not fully verified: the file tree came truncated (very large repository).
depth.treeUnavailable: ? Configuration not verified: the file tree could not be fetched.
depth.listingIncomplete: ? Configuration not fully verified: the listing of some AI configuration directory failed.

aiProcess.commitsTooltip: Recent non-merge commits, without maintenance bots (Dependabot, Renovate…), with declared AI co-authorship or authored by an agent.
aiProcess.prsTooltip: Latest merged PRs, without maintenance bots, authored by a coding agent (Copilot, Claude, Devin…).
aiProcess.aiReviewedTooltip: Merged PRs with at least one review or comment from an AI review bot (CodeRabbit, Copilot, Gemini…).

safeguards.title: Safeguards
safeguards.agentUnapproved: {{unapproved}} of {{agentPrs}} agent PRs merged without human approval
safeguards.noAgentPrs: No agent PRs in the sample: nothing to check.
safeguards.size: Median size: agents {{agent}} lines (n = {{agentN}}) × people {{human}} lines (n = {{humanN}})
safeguards.sizeUnavailable: The size comparison needs at least {{min}} PRs of known size in each group (agents: {{agentN}}, people: {{humanN}}).
safeguards.tooltip: Human approval: an APPROVED review before the merge, by someone who is not the author and not a bot (same rule as Code Review).

coherence.title: The sources disagree
coherence.intro: This repository's trace sources tell different stories. That proves nothing: see the possible causes.
coherence.configWithoutDeclaration: There is versioned AI configuration (outside the template), but no commit in the sample declares AI co-authorship or is authored by an agent.
coherence.hiddenWithoutDeclaration: .gitignore ignores AI artifacts (unversioned local use), but no commit in the sample declares AI co-authorship.
coherence.toolMismatch: The configuration is for one tool and the declarations are from another (informational, not a disagreement).
coherence.coauthorDisabled: Declaration turned off in the configuration: the versioned .claude/settings.json turns off Claude Code's co-author trailer.

legitimateCauses.squash: squash merges that rewrite commit messages;
legitimateCauses.otherMember: configuration set up by another group member;
legitimateCauses.noTrailer: a tool that does not write the co-author trailer;
legitimateCauses.disabled: declaration turned off in the tool's configuration.

coherence.commitsUnverified: commits (recent commits could not be fetched)
coherence.gitignoreUnverified: .gitignore and turned-off declaration (AI context query unavailable)
coherence.templateUnverified: template origin (it couldn't be confirmed which configuration files came from the template or from GitHub Classroom)
coherence.prsUnverified: PRs (merged PRs could not be fetched)

badge.title: Responsible AI use
badge.tooltip: Checks observable practices and coherence between AI traces, not actual AI use nor anyone's character. Criteria that were not verified or do not apply are left out of the count. It does not penalize not using AI.

unavailable.noToken: With a GitHub token, we also check .gitignore, configuration (turned-off declaration), template, AI review and safeguards.
unavailable.error: Part of the data could not be fetched (GitHub API failure or limit): items marked N/A or ? were not verified.

aiProcess.notRecorded: AI in the Process: not recorded in this analysis.

students.title: Per student
students.notice: Shows only AI use declared in commits (co-authorship) and who configured AI tools in the repository. Configuring is not the same as using: in a group, one person may set up the configuration for everyone. Undeclared use does not show up here, so no record does not mean no use. Do not use this data as a grade or as proof.
students.agentLimit: People who use cloud agents may show less declared AI than they used: commits made by the agent itself appear in the agent's row.
students.unavailable: The period's commits could not be fetched.
students.empty: No commits in the period (merges and maintenance bots excluded).
students.sampled: Computed over the 300 most recent commits of the period.
students.configUnavailable: n/a: could not check who added or changed the AI configuration files.
students.footnote: Default-branch commits in the period, without merges and maintenance bots. "Unidentified author" gathers commits not linked to a GitHub account (we don't group by name). Configuration: AI files (template files excluded) with a commit by that person in the period, in the checked locations. Nothing in this table is saved or goes into the CSV.
